name: Light Pink
lede: Light Pink is the web's name for a pale, slightly warm pink, one of the 140 colors in the X11 set and later in CSS, with the hex code #FFB6C1.

sections.title: A plain name in a long list
sections.body:
Light Pink is one of the 140 colors in the X11 Color Set, and its hex code is #FFB6C1 [1]. It entered the CSS color list, which is why every browser knows it by name [2]. The word *light* here is only a descriptor: dictionaries of color have long used "a light pink" as the plain gloss for older words such as *incarnate*, meaning flesh-colored, and *rosebud* [1].

The screen value is a convention, not a measured sample. The German RAL system has a pink of its own, RAL 3015, first issued in 1927, and its screen approximation is a deeper, duller pink than the web's [3]. Our library also lists Soft Pink and Cherry Blossom Pink within about two units of color difference of this swatch, so the three names can be used almost interchangeably [3]. Its nearest neighbors in the app are [[baby-pink]] and [[pink]], and the loud opposite is [[hot-pink]].

sections.title: How pink got its meaning
sections.body:
Light pinks are a modern idea. Pastoureau places the rise of the pink we know in the middle of the eighteenth century, when it was finally understood as a mixture of red and white rather than a kind of yellow [4]. Madame de Pompadour made it fashionable for rooms and furnishings, often paired with sky blue [4]. In French, *rose* as a color adjective did not appear in dictionaries before the mid-eighteenth century, and the Académie Française's dictionary did not include it until 1835 [4].

The English word *pink* is also relatively young, St Clair notes [5]. In the Enlightenment pink was not reserved for girls, and many boys wore it until the end of the nineteenth century [4].

A common belief says that pink has always belonged to girls and blue to boys. That is a myth. A New York Times article of 1893 stated the rule the other way round, and a trade publication in 1918 still called pink the stronger color and blue the more delicate [5]. The reversal settled only in the mid-twentieth century [4][5].

sections.title: Where the plain words appear
sections.body:
Because *light pink* is descriptive, it turns up wherever a writer needs a quick label. Finlay reports that Aboriginal artists of Arnhem Land, in a list recorded by the researcher George Chaloupka, name a light pink among eight main paint colors, beside black, yellows, a red made by burning yellow, and a shiny hematite red [6]. In the Paterson dictionary the same two words gloss several older terms, but no single pigment or dye carries the name [1].

That is why the honest history of this swatch is short. Its date is the date of the X11 and CSS lists, and the pale pink in a rose petal, a ballet shoe or a baby blanket is a different thing under the same word [1][2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, this exact pink covers a meaningful share of the canvas in 2 paintings, which is 0.01 per cent, rarer than 86 per cent of the named colors, as photographed [7]. That is thin evidence for the family of pale pinks, because this count is only for a close match to one swatch [7]. In printed English the phrase peaks in the 1930s, and it rose fastest in the 1880s [8]. The Google Books count includes every sense of the words, so it is a rough guide [8].
